interactions.summary: Jiang resolves the Jephthah paradox by saying God is love itself, so sacrificing the daughter would betray God rather than obey him, and any rash vow that asks for harm would simply be ignored by God.

A student proposes that God gives human beings an inner vaccine against such vows and uses free will to explain how connection to God can be lost, while Jiang keeps pressing for the concrete reason Jephthah would sever that connection in the first place.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student free-will hypothesis with Jiang pressure

claims.claim: Jiang says true faith begins with understanding God's nature, and because God is first and foremost love, killing one's daughter is not obedience to God but treachery against love itself.

Jiang extends the same logic to the bank-robbery analogy: refusing a beloved's destructive demand can be the real act of love, while compliance would reveal possessiveness and the desire to control rather than love.

Jiang argues that a rash vow to kill the first person through the door would simply be ignored by God, because such a promise comes from misunderstanding God and therefore does not establish a real covenantal connection.

A student proposes that God has put a kind of preventive understanding in human beings, so people make ungodly vows only when they have not really taken in that divine protection or been in contact with God.

The student's next move is to explain the break with God through free will and self-formation, but Jiang rejects that as too abstract and keeps demanding the concrete cause of Jephthah's loss of connection.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang imagines God talking back to Jephthah in plain speech: I do not want this garbage from you, because murder cannot be the tribute of love.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i don't want this crap from you
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's most vivid compression of Jiang's theology: the paradox dissolves once God is understood as love rather than as a sovereign who craves sacrificial displays.

signature_moments.moment: Refusal becomes the proof of love, while criminal obedience becomes the sign that one wants to possess and control the beloved.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it's because i love you that i'm not going to do this
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's clean reversal: Jiang turns sacrificial compliance from devotion into betrayal and makes refusal the morally faithful act.

signature_moments.moment: A student reaches for a medical image and calls divine understanding a vaccine against catastrophic vows.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The metaphor is memorable and shows the seminar trying to explain how moral knowledge works before Jiang redirects the issue toward the concrete lure of power.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's governing theological axiom for resolving the Jephthah paradox: any vow that degrades love cannot be an authentic command from God.
A vow made out of misunderstanding, spiritual disconnection, or impulsive bargaining, which Jiang says God would simply ignore rather than enforce.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet completes the shift from the modern love analogy back into theology: Jiang explicitly equates God with love, rejects destructive vow-keeping as betrayal, and then steers the class toward the deeper question of why someone would sever that loving connection at all.
